name: Esther Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing electronic and software engineering in Glasgow, and I live in a flat with two girls from church, Abena and Grace. My week is lectures, a circuits lab on Wednesdays, and choir practice on Thursday nights. On Sundays we all go to the Ghanaian congregation, and afterwards there's food and a lot of talking. My mum runs a catering business and my dad owns a pharmacy, and they pay for my degree and my rent. I use an AI tool now and then when a lab report's structure confuses me, but I write the content myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with five pictures of the next few years. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I thought, there's a lot of talk and little change. At church the older ones would say they told us so, and I'd smile. I'd say people should still work hard, because hard work wins in any world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel fine about my degree, but I'd still carry my parents' worries about costs. Mum's catering depends on events, and events depend on people having spare money. Dad's pharmacy is steady, but the supplier prices keep going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on studying and use my free time to help Mum at weekend events, because she pays me and it's useful experience. I'd look for a summer placement at an engineering firm, and I'd keep singing in the choir. I'd also save part of what Mum pays me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. The world stays normal, but normal isn't easy for my family's businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said normal isn't easy. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said normal isn't easy. What do you mean? Mum's margins are thin. A wedding for 200 people can make or lose my mum a month's income, and one cancellation hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What do you do to help? I keep the spreadsheet of orders for her, and I think I could build a simple booking app for her. It would be my first real project.

say: I'd say there's a lot of **talk** and little change.
I'd say people should still **work hard**, because hard work wins in any world.
think: I'm fine about my degree, but I still carry my parents' **cost worries**.
Mum's catering depends on events and **people's spare money**.
do: Help Mum at **weekend events**, for pay and experience.
Look for a summer **placement** at an engineering firm.
Save part of what **Mum pays me**.
feel: **Uneasy** a little; normal isn't easy for my family's businesses.
S0.quote: A wedding for 200 people can make or lose my mum a month's income, and one cancellation hurts.
fieldNote: Esther's unease is **ordinary pressure** on her parents' small businesses.
She already keeps Mum's order spreadsheet and sees a first real project.
Faith and hard work are her framework.

steps.text: Work weekend events for my mum's catering business
Apply for a summer placement at an engineering firm
Save a third of what my mum pays me

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming and we should work with it. At church I'd say the Lord gave us minds to use, and a young person who learns the tools will be useful. And I'd tell Dad to look at what the pharmacy can automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think my own field, writing code and checking designs, is where the machines go first. But I'd also think there'll be new jobs, and I'm good at picking things up when I see they work. My worry is the juniors, since fewer firms will pay people to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools properly, not just for report structure. I'd show Mum how to use a tool for her menus and quotes, because it saves her evenings. And I'd start small side jobs, building simple websites for church members' businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also a bit proud. I'd be one of the people helping others, and that's a good place to stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help your mum with menus?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How would you help your mum with menus? A tool could draft the quote from her event notes and I'd check it. She does them at midnight now and she's tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would your dad say? He'd say pharmacy is regulated and humans must check, which is true. But he'd also say, look, the dispensing robot at the big chain is cheaper, so we must be better at talking to people.

say: I'd say it's coming and we should **work with it**.
I'd say young people who learn the tools will be **useful**.
think: My own field, **writing code** and checking designs, is where machines go first.
The worry is **juniors**, since fewer firms pay people to learn.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly, not just for report structure.
Show Mum a tool for her **menus and quotes**.
Build simple **websites** for church members' businesses.
feel: **Uneasy** but a little proud to be helping others.
S1.quote: The Lord gave us minds to use, and a young person who learns the tools will be useful.
fieldNote: She wants to use her skills to help her mum's late-night workload.
Her dad's answer: be better at talking to people.

steps.text: Set up an AI quote draft for my mum's catering events
Build websites for two church members' small businesses
Take the machine learning module in second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should hold on to what makes us human and look after one another. In the church we'd organise help for families, because government will be too slow. And I'd say publicly that businesses and families that plan will cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be scared. My degree would be useless fast, and my parents' pharmacy would feel it too, because the dispensing and ordering are thinking work. Mum's catering lasts longer, since the kitchens are hands-on until robots arrive in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the degree, because I made a promise to my parents. I'd work with Mum more, learn the business side, and start a small enterprise of my own. I'd ask Dad to reduce costs now, so the pharmacy has a cushion, and I'd pray every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel my heart beat quickly when I check the news. At the same time I'd feel a quiet, strong belief that we've come through hard times before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of enterprise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What kind of enterprise? Probably something with food and tech, like an ordering system for small caterers. I know what Mum goes through, and other caterers are in the same position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Abena and Grace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell Abena and Grace? To stay together as a flat and share food and costs. We could cook together and no one would starve, and that's a real plan, not just a nice thought.

say: I'd say **hold on** to what makes us human and look after one another.
At church we'd organise **help for families**.
think: My degree would be **useless fast**, and the pharmacy's thinking work too.
Mum's catering lasts **longer**, since kitchens are hands-on until 2031.
do: Stay in the degree, because I **promised** my parents.
Learn the **business side** of Mum's catering and start my own small enterprise.
Ask Dad to **cut costs** now so the pharmacy has a cushion.
feel: **Anxious**, with a quiet belief that we've come through hard times.
S2.quote: We've come through hard times before.
fieldNote: Faith and community are her **safety net**, alongside a real plan.
She sees catering as safer for longer than the pharmacy.
She'd start a small ordering system for caterers.

steps.text: Learn the books and ordering side of my mum's catering
Build an ordering tool for small caterers in Glasgow
Ask my dad to cut pharmacy costs and build a reserve
Organise shared meals with Abena, Grace and church families

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare and short enough to take seriously. I'd tell friends to build something now, not wait. At church I'd say let's start a young professionals' group to share jobs and tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel it's a sharp bend, but one I can steer. I'd graduate in 2029 and AGI arrives 2031, so I'd have two years to establish myself. My enterprise could be running by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and do a placement at a firm that builds electronics, which is hands-on. I'd build the caterers' ordering tool and try to get ten customers before graduation. And I'd put aside money for Mum's business in case a tough year comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel a mix of purpose and tiredness, because I'd be doing a lot at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save for your mum's business. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd save for your mum's business. Why? My mum took risks for me, and now I can protect her business. A cushion of two months of costs would let her breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to do all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you cut to do all this? Time, mostly. I'd drop one choir night a week, which would hurt, and I'd say no to some social things.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare and **short enough** to take seriously.
I'd start a young professionals' group at **church**.
think: It's a **sharp bend**, but one I can steer.
I'd have **two years** after graduating to establish myself before AGI.
do: Do a **placement** at a firm that builds electronics.
Get **ten customers** for the caterers' ordering tool before graduating.
Save **two months** of costs for Mum's business.
feel: **Uneasy**, with purpose and tiredness mixed together.
S3.quote: My mum took risks for me, and now I can protect her business.
fieldNote: Her plan is built around **protecting her mum's business**.
She trades time and a choir night for progress.
Five years gives her time to test an enterprise.

steps.text: Do an electronics placement at a firm near Glasgow
Sign up ten caterers for the ordering tool before graduating
Save two months of costs for my mum's business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing if we use it well. I'd say that church, family and honest work matter even more when the world changes. And I'd say that young people should build, not complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel calm. I'd be 28 in 2036, probably with a few years of work, a small business, and maybe a family. It would be a normal life for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work at an engineering firm for a few years, and keep building the ordering tool into a proper company. I'd learn each new AI tool when it's shown to work. And I'd keep tithing and saving, which is how my parents taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and thankful. I'd still pray about it, because change is change, but I wouldn't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you lose sleep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make you lose sleep? If my parents' businesses failed or my church community scattered. Money I can rebuild, but people moving away is harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to say to people your age then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you want to say to people your age then? Don't wait for permission. Start small, save regularly, and pick friends who tell you the truth.

say: I'd say ten years is a **blessing** if we use it well.
I'd say young people should **build**, not complain.
think: I'd be 28 in 2036 with years of work, a **small business** and maybe a family.
It would be a **normal life** for a long time.
do: Work at an **engineering firm** for a few years.
Grow the ordering tool into a proper **company**.
Keep **tithing and saving**, as my parents taught me.
feel: **Calm** and thankful, though I'd still pray about it.
S4.quote: Don't wait for permission. Start small, save regularly, and pick friends who tell you the truth.
fieldNote: With a decade, Esther sees an **ordinary good life**.
Her sleep risk is people scattering, not technology.
She names advice she'd give peers: start small, save and pick honest friends.

steps.text: Work three years at an engineering firm after graduating
Turn the caterers' ordering tool into a registered company
Save and give a fixed share of every pay cheque

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time and my degree and my dad's pharmacy would both be hit first. The longer ones give me room to build something. What would help is community, honest information and a way for small businesses like my mum's to use the tools without paying a fortune.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not afraid of work, I'm afraid of not having time to get ready.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of work, I'm afraid of not having time to get ready.
portrait: Esther is an 18-year-old **electronic and software engineering** student in Glasgow, active in her Ghanaian church and choir.
Her mum's catering business and her dad's pharmacy pay for her studies, so her **cushion is strong**.
She is traditional and steady: she trusts **hard work**, **faith** and community, and uses AI tools when proven.
She plans to build an **ordering tool** for caterers and to protect her family's businesses.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, since her degree and her dad's pharmacy would be hit first.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **community support**, honest information and cheap tools for small businesses like her mum's.
